title: Study on the rising trend of groundwater levels in Beijing and its impact on underground space
content:
by Hongli Mu, Yanlin Li, Shiqing Wang, Han Zhu

Most large and medium-sized cities in China are water-deficient. Long-term overexploitation of groundwater has led to the deterioration of the urban geo-environment, whereas recent measures such as ecological water replenishment and groundwater abstraction control have substantially alleviated this trend. However, groundwater level rise may also cause damage to underground space and affect the development and utilization of underground space resources. Taking the Beijing Plain as an example, this study investigates the trend and patterns of urban groundwater level rise from 2019 to 2025, as well as its impact on the development and utilization of underground space. On this basis, groundwater regulation countermeasures are examined using the marginal analysis method from environmental economics. The results show that ecological water replenishment in Beijing has raised the average groundwater level in the urban plain area by 14.81 m compared with that in 2015. Groundwater level rise exerts multiple damage effects on existing underground space structures, including structural corrosion and deterioration, leakage, anti-uplift failure, increased foundation settlement, and differential hydrostatic pressure-induced damage. It also increases groundwater-related disaster risks during the construction of underground engineering projects and increases the costs of construction dewatering and groundwater cutoff measures. Through a comprehensive benefit analysis of groundwater level rise, this study proposes a multi-level prevention and control framework comprising “dynamic regulation of rising groundwater levels, improvement of anti-uplift design standards, enhancement of underground space resilience, optimization of groundwater control technologies for underground engineering, and establishment of a groundwater level monitoring and early-warning mechanism.” This framework can provide a scientific basis for establishing a reasonable urban ecological water replenishment mechanism and achieving the sustainable development and utilization of underground space.
